posts.t:
hoeschec wrote: G/J

I am posting this chart for now, but will follow up with an explanation for why I don't want to trade this QM.

OK, so here were my thoughts on this setup on Thursday (the QM actually ended up working nicely, so maybe I am wrong in my analysis). Many times when a QM fails, I notice the 'engulf' part of the HH or LL doesn't engulf the important flag to the left. This G/J was a good example of a QM that I didn't think engulfed the correct flag. To me, the flag (blue rectangle) is the flag that held price down, and also was the origin of the move that created the new low. To me, this was the important flag to engulf. For that reason, I didn't want to take the long when price returned to the QM level.

Either the setup worked just out of dumb luck, or I mis-read the chart.

IF just posted an amazing trade on his journal USD/JPY.

I am going to figure out why he took the trade so I can keep an eye out for similar opportunities in the future.

By going out to a weekly chart I see a previous QM level. Did IF take the trade because price returned to this level, or is there more to it?

Here is the Weekly Chart

Here is the Daily Chart - This is a zoomed in area that the QM originally formed. I noticed a key FTR that formed (labeled on the chart). The red dashed line is the location of IF's trade yesterday. Did IF take yesterday's short based off of this previous QM short, assuming there would be left over orders at this level?

If this is the rational for IF's trade, how did he know there would be a reaction at this level? I have seen price return to previous QM levels before, and there has not been a reaction like this. What am I not seeing about this setup that made it worth trading? Is there another important factor that I need to look for to increase the odds of a setup like this working out?

Yes, I think that's a good explanation. There was always a good chance that the nearest QM would FO given the close proximity of the larger QM above. Also, I don't have less than H4 data here, but look at the large candle down (big DP to sell) after the QM's HH. I think if we could drill down in LTF into this we could pinpoint the sell point? There's other strong decisions to sell on that chart that produce big reactions on FTB

EDIT - oh one thing I forgot to add. I remember reading a comment (I think from IF) ----when u see 2 high peaks quite close together and reaching a similar level (like on the chart, then it's very common for a third peak to be made above them which turn out to be the selloff point. Psychology at play - the 2 highs form a resistance to be sold into. The peak above take's out those shorts and adds some breakout buyer buys... all the more yummy sells for the big seller to get on:-)

posts.t:
Actually, after going back to IF's USD/JPY trade, I still have some questions. On the chart below, I have drawn a red, blue, and green arrow. All three of these arrows show where price pierced the FL which made up the first shoulder of the QM. What steps can a trader make to not get caught taking a trade at the red or the blue arrow?

The red and blue arrow both pierce the FL, however taking a short at that point would require a substantial SL. Is the solution as simple as only taking the short if price will retrace far enough in to the FL that the SL is low enough and R:R is high enough? There are tons of examples where a QM setup works and price turns immediately after piercing the limit the of the FL. Is there a way to differentiate which QM's will react immediately to price entering a QM and which QM's will react only after price retraces deep in to the FL?

With regard to decision points, I think a legitimate argument can be made that the red and blue arrows are reacting to important decision points as well. The red arrow shows price reacting the a S/R level and alos the DP where price breaks out of the lower limit of the FL. Similar situation with the blue arrow. Why is the DP @ the green arrow the one IF waited to take a trade at? What makes that DP more important than the ones the red and blue arrows are reacting to?

در واقع، بعد از برگشت به معاملهٔ USD/JPY مربوط به IF، هنوز چند سؤال دارم. روی چارت پایین، پیکان‌های قرمز، آبی و سبز کشیده‌ام. هر سه این پیکان‌ها جایی را نشان می‌دهند که قیمت FL را شکست که شانهٔ اول QM را می‌ساخت. چه مراحلی می‌تواند یک معامله‌گر انجام دهد تا در گرفتن معامله روی پیکان قرمز یا آبی به دام نیفتد؟

پیکان قرمز و آبی هر دو FL را می‌شکنند، با این حال فروش‌گرفتن در آن نقطه SL قابل‌توجهی می‌خواست. آیا راه‌حل به همین سادگی است که فقط اگر قیمت به‌اندازهٔ کافی به داخل FL برگردد که SL به‌اندازهٔ کافی پایین و R:R به‌اندازهٔ کافی بالا باشد فروش بگیریم؟ مثال‌های زیادی هست که یک ستاپ QM کار می‌کند و قیمت بلافاصله بعد از شکست حد FL می‌چرخد. آیا راهی برای تشخیص اینکه کدام QM‌ها بلافاصله به ورود قیمت در QM واکنش نشان می‌دهند و کدام QM‌ها فقط بعد از برگشت عمیق قیمت به داخل FL واکنش نشان می‌دهند وجود دارد؟

در رابطه با نقاط تصمیم‌گیری، فکر می‌کنم می‌توان استدلال معتبری کرد که پیکان‌های قرمز و آبی هم به نقاط تصمیم‌گیری مهم واکنش نشان می‌دهند. پیکان قرمز قیمت را در حال واکنش به یک سطح S/R و همچنین DP‌ی که قیمت از حد پایین FL بیرون می‌زند نشان می‌دهد. وضعیت مشابه با پیکان آبی. چرا DP @ پیکان سبز همان است که IF منتظرش ماند تا معامله کند؟ چه چیزی آن DP را از DP‌هایی که پیکان‌های قرمز و آبی به آن‌ها واکنش نشان می‌دهند مهم‌تر می‌کند؟

این جزئیات واقعاً مهمی هستند که فکر می‌کنم نیاز به بحث دارند چون می‌توانند تفاوت بین یک معاملهٔ شکست‌خورده و یک معاملهٔ موفق را بسازند.

ایده‌ها؟
